Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 66, verse 1:

Surat al-Tahrim

It is also called Surat al-Mutaharrim, Surat Lima Tuharrim, and Surat al-Nabi (ﷺ). It is also reported from Ibn al-Zubayr that it is called Surat al-Nisa' (the Chapter of the Women). The well-known view is that it is Madani. It is reported from Qatadah that the Madani part of it extends to the end of the tenth verse, and the rest is Makki. Its number of verses is twelve by consensus. It resembles the surah before it in opening with an address to the Prophet (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him). The earlier surah deals with the divorce of wives, and this one deals with the prohibition (of something) concerning the slave-girls, and the connection between them is clear. Since the earlier surah dealt with the disputes of the wives of the Ummah, this one mentions the disputes of the wives of the Chosen Prophet (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him), to magnify their station, so that they are not mentioned alongside all other women; hence they were given a surah of their own. For this reason it ends with the mention of the two spouses of the Prophet (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him) in Paradise, Asiyah the wife of Pharaoh and Maryam the daughter of 'Imran. This is what al-Jalal al-Suyuti (may Allah have mercy on him) said.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾ Al-Bukhari, Ibn Sa'd, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'A'ishah: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to stay with Zaynab bint Jahsh and drink honey there. So I and Hafsah agreed that whichever of us the Prophet (ﷺ) entered upon first, she would say: 'I smell from you the odour of maghafir. Have you eaten maghafir?' He entered upon one of them and she said that to him. He said: 'No, rather I drank honey at the house of Zaynab bint Jahsh, and I will not return to it.'" In another narration: "And I have sworn, so do not tell anyone about that." Then the verse was revealed: ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit﴾ and so on. In another narration: "Sawdah said: 'Have you eaten maghafir?' He said: 'No.' She said: 'Then what is this smell I notice from you?' He said: 'Hafsah gave me a drink of honey.' She said: 'You have grazed on the nahlat al-'Urfut (the bee of the 'urfut tree).'" So he prohibited honey, and then the verse was revealed. In a hadith narrated by al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i from 'A'ishah: he drank honey in the house of Hafsah, and the one who said it was Sawdah and Safiyyah.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, and al-Hafiz al-Suyuti said: with a sound chain, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) drank a drink of honey at the house of Sawdah. He then entered upon 'A'ishah and she said: 'I notice a smell from you.' He entered upon Hafsah and she said: 'I notice a smell from you.' He said: 'I think it is from a drink I drank at Sawdah's. By Allah, I will not drink it.'" Then the verse was revealed.

Al-Nasa'i and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had a slave-girl with whom he had intercourse, but 'A'ishah and Hafsah did not cease to pressure him until he made her forbidden to himself. So Allah revealed this verse: ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit﴾ and so on." This is supported by what al-Bazzar and al-Tabarani narrated with a good, sound chain from Ibn 'Abbas who said: the verse ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit﴾ was revealed concerning his slave-girl.

The well-known view is that she was Mariyah, and that he (peace be upon him) had intercourse with her in the house of Hafsah on her day, and Hafsah found out and reproached him. He (ﷺ) said: "Are you not pleased that I make her forbidden, so that I do not approach her?" She said: "Yes," and so he made her forbidden. In another narration, that this took place in the house of Hafsah on the day of 'A'ishah. In al-Kashshaf it is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was alone with Mariyah on the day of 'A'ishah, and Hafsah learned of it, so he said to her: "Keep it secret for me. I have made Mariyah forbidden to myself, and I give you the glad tidings that Abu Bakr and 'Umar will rule the affairs of my Ummah after me." So she informed 'A'ishah, and the two were close friends.

In sum, the reports conflict, and you have heard what has been said about them. However, al-Khafaji said: al-Nawawi said in his commentary on Muslim: "The correct view is that the verse concerns the story of the honey, not the story of Mariyah, which is narrated outside the two Sahihs, and the story of Mariyah has not come through a sound route." Then al-Khafaji said, also quoting him: "The correct view is that the drinking of honey was at the house of Zaynab, may Allah be pleased with her." Al-Tibi said, regarding what we quoted from al-Kashshaf: I have not found it in the well-known books, and Allah knows best.

Al-Maghafir: with a fatha on the mim and the ghayn pointed, and a ya after the fa, according to what al-Qadi 'Iyad preferred, is the plural of maghfur (with a damma on the mim), a thing that has a foul smell, exuded by the 'urfut, which is a tree or plant with broad leaves. According to al-Mutli', the 'urfut is gum, and the maghfur is a thorn that has blossoms from which bees feed, on which the 'urfut appears. The Prophet (ﷺ) greatly loved fragrance and disliked foul odours, owing to the refinement of his noble soul and because the angel would come to him while he disliked them. So what was said grieved him (peace be upon him), and what happened, happened. In his address (ﷺ) with "O Prophet" at the opening of the reproach, there is what is evident of gentle kindness towards him and of honouring his lofty position (peace be upon him). A parallel to this is the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Allah pardon you; why did you grant them permission?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 43]. The meaning of "prohibit" is abstaining. And by "what Allah has made lawful" is honey, according to what al-Nawawi (may Allah have mercy on him) regarded as sound, or intercourse with his slave-girl according to some narrations. The reason for the expression "what" in these two explanations is evident.

Some have explained "what" as referring to Mariyah, and the expression "what" for her follows the common usage of referring to what the right hand possesses; the point in it is not hidden. The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿seeking the pleasure of your wives﴾, are a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of ﴿prohibit﴾, and Abu Hayyan preferred this. In that case, it is the locus of the reproach, according to what has been said. The likely reason is that a statement containing a restriction, where the restriction is the intended focus, whether affirmed or negated, or the restriction is of the type "multiplied manifold", on the basis that prohibition in itself is a matter for reproach and its motive is likewise, as in al-Kashf. Or it is a grammatical or explanatory resumption (istie'naf), and this is the preferable view. Its reasoning is that the interrogation is not literal, but is rather a reproach for the fact that the prohibition did not arise from a praiseworthy motive, so it was appropriate to ask about what is disapproved, and others among the prophets (peace be upon them) have done this. Do you not see the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿except what Israel made unlawful for himself﴾ [Al 'Imran: 93]? Then it was said: ﴿seeking the pleasure of your wives﴾, and "someone like you, of such high rank, should not seek their pleasure in such a way." It is also permitted that it be an explanation of "prohibit", by making the seeking of their pleasure the very prohibition, as an exaggeration of its being its cause, and in this is what is in it of magnifying the matter. The annexation in "your wives" is for the genus, not for totality.

﴿And Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾. In this is an exaltation of his (ﷺ) station: that leaving the better course, in relation to his lofty and noble rank, counts as a sin, even though in itself it is not so; and that his reproof (ﷺ) is only for greater care for him. Al-Zamakhshari slipped here, as is his habit, claiming that what occurred was the prohibition of a lawful matter that was forbidden, but that he (peace be upon him) was forgiven for it. Ibn al-Munir in al-Intisaf launched a strong attack upon him in condemnation, saying in substance: what he attributed concerning the Prophet (ﷺ) is a fabrication and calumny, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) is innocent of it. This is because the prohibition of what is lawful is of two kinds. The first is believing that the ruling of prohibition is established regarding it, which is like believing that the ruling of permissibility applies to the forbidden, which is a prohibited act entailing disbelief, so it is impossible that it should proceed from the infallible at all. The second is abstaining from the lawful absolutely, or emphatically by oath, while believing it to be lawful; this is pure permissibility and pure lawfulness. Were abstaining from what is permissible itself not permissible, the reality of lawfulness would be nullified. What occurred from him (ﷺ) was of this type, and Allah reproached him only out of gentleness towards him, and as a token of his worth and honouring his station (peace be upon him), that he should take account of the pleasure of his wives by means of what grieved him, in keeping with the gentle kindness of Allah the Exalted towards him, which was customary. Some have interpreted al-Zamakhshari's words, but there is in them what is repugnant to this.

It has been said: attributing the prohibition to him (ﷺ) is metaphorical, and the meaning is "why do you become a cause for Allah the Exalted to prohibit for you what He has made lawful for you, by your oath to abandon it." This is not in need of this. Regarding the occurrence of the oath there is disagreement, and whoever holds that it occurred relies on some reports and on the apparent meaning

**His saying, Exalted is He:** ﴿Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution (*taḥillah*) of your oaths﴾, meaning He has prescribed for you their dissolution (*taḥlīl*), which is the release from what oaths have bound, through expiation (*kaffārah*). So *taḥillah* is a verbal noun of *ḥallala*, like *takrimah* from *karrama*, and it is not the regular verbal noun. The regular one is *taḥlīl* and *takrīm*, since the standard verbal noun of the *faʻʻala* pattern with a sound middle radical that is not hamzated is *tafʻīl*. Its original form was *taḥlilah*, which was contracted by assimilation (*idghām*). It derives from *ḥill*, the opposite of *ʻaqd* (binding). Thus, by swearing an oath on something, one binds oneself to it by commitment, and by expiation that binding is undone. It is also undone by affirming the oath, as in the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "No man loses three children and is then touched by the Fire, except as a *taḥillat al-qasam*," meaning ﴿And there is none of you but will pass through it﴾ [Maryam 19:71], and so on. Its dissolution is also achieved by the smallest amount that the word applies to: for example, one who swears that he will "descend" is satisfied by a brief passing-through. Thus the expression is a metaphor for minimisation, i.e., the amount of a brief passing. It is also undone by the *istithnāʼ* (exception clause, i.e., the oath-taker saying "if Allah wills"), with its known condition in jurisprudence.

It is understood from the words of al-Kashshāf that *taḥlīl* can mean *istithnāʼ*. Its meaning, as in al-Kashf, is the placing of the exception immediately after the oath, when unrestricted, so that it does not take effect. From this comes the phrase *ḥalā abayta al-laʻn* ("may you refuse the curse"). According to the view that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had made an oath, as some reports state, and this is the apparent meaning of the verse, scholars differed over whether he (ﷺ) gave expiation or not. Al-Ḥasan (al-Baṣrī) said that he (ﷺ) did not give expiation, because his past and future sins had been forgiven, and this was only a teaching for the believers. But the objection to this is that forgiveness of sins is not a valid proof, because the worldly legal consequences of his (ﷺ) action are not a matter of being held accountable for a sin; moreover, it is not agreed that it was a sin. It is reported from Muqātil that the Prophet (ﷺ) freed a slave in connection with the prohibition of Māriyah. Mālik, in al-Mudawwanah, transmitted from Zayd ibn Aslam that the Prophet (ﷺ) gave expiation for his prohibition of his umm walad (slave-concubine who bore him a child) when he swore that he would not approach her. Similar is reported from al-Shaʻbī.

The scholars differed over the ruling on a man's saying to his wife, "You are unlawful to me (*anti ʻalayya ḥarām*)" or "What is lawful to me is unlawful," without making an exception for his wife. It was said that a group of scholars, including Masrūq, Rabīʻah, Abū Salamah, al-Shaʻbī and Aṣbagh, held that it is like prohibiting water or food: nothing is incumbent upon him. Abū Bakr, ʻUmar, Zayd, Ibn Masʻūd, Ibn ʻAbbās, ʻĀʼishah, Ibn al-Musayyib, ʻAṭāʼ, Ṭāwūs, Sulaymān ibn Yasār, Ibn Jubayr, Qatādah, al-Ḥasan, al-Awzāʻī, Abū Thawr and a group (of scholars) held that it is an oath for which one makes expiation. Ibn ʻAbbās also held this in one narration, and al-Shāfiʻī in one of his two opinions held that it requires expiation for an oath but is not itself an oath. Abū Ḥanīfah holds that the prohibition of a lawful thing is an oath in every case, and the intended benefit of what he prohibits is taken into account. So if he prohibits food, it is an oath not to eat it; if a slave-girl, an oath not to have intercourse with her; if a wife, it is an *īlāʼ* (oath of abstention) from her, if he has no intention. If he intends *ẓihār* (the pre-Islamic declaration likening the wife to his mother's back), it is *ẓihār*; if he intends divorce, it is an irrevocable divorce; likewise if he intends two, it is two; if he intends three, it is three, as he intended. If he says, "I intended a lie," he is believed between himself and Allah, but not in the judgement of the judge to annul the *īlāʼ*, because the utterance is considered a performative act by custom. Others said: if he intends nothing, it is an oath.

In *al-Taḥrīr*, Abū Ḥanīfah and his companions said: if he intends divorce, it is one irrevocable divorce; or if two, it is one; or if three, it is three. Or if he intends nothing, he is an *mūlī* (one who has made an *īlāʼ*). Or if *ẓihār*, it is *ẓihār*. Ibn al-Qāsim said: the intention of *ẓihār* does not benefit him, and it is divorce. Yaḥyā ibn ʻUmar said: it is as such; if he takes her back, it is not permissible for him to have intercourse with her until he makes the expiation of *ẓihār*, and what he intended of divorce takes effect. If he intended one, it is revocable, and this is one opinion of al-Shāfiʻī. Al-Awzāʻī, Sufyān and Abū Thawr said: whatever form of divorce he intended takes effect; if he intended nothing, Sufyān said: nothing is incumbent upon him, while al-Awzāʻī and Abū Thawr said: one (revocable divorce) takes effect. Ibn Jubayr said: he must free a slave, even if it is not *ẓihār*. Abū Qilābah, ʻUthmān, Aḥmad and Isḥāq said: the prohibition is *ẓihār*, so its expiation is due. From al-Shāfiʻī: if he intended that she is prohibited like his mother's back, it is *ẓihār*; or the prohibition of her person without divorce; or if he intended nothing, it is the expiation of an oath. Mālik said: three (divorces) take effect for a woman who has been consummated, and whatever he intended of one or two (is what takes effect); three take effect for one not consummated. Ibn Abī Laylā and ʻAbd al-Malik ibn al-Mājishūn said: three take effect in both cases. Ibn Khuwayzimandād transmitted from Mālik, and Zayd and Ḥammād ibn Abī Sulaymān said: one irrevocable divorce takes effect in both cases. al-Zuhrī and ʻAbd al-ʻAzīz ibn al-Mājishūn said: one revocable divorce. Abū Muṣʻab and Muḥammad ibn ʻAbd al-Ḥakam said: one takes effect for the woman not consummated, and three for the one consummated.

In *al-Kashshāf* it is said: al-Shāfiʻī does not consider it an oath, but a cause of expiation in the case of women alone. As for divorce, it is revocable according to him. From ʻAlī, may Allah honour his face, (the ruling is) three. From Zayd, one irrevocable. From ʻUthmān, *ẓihār*. Al-Bukhārī, Muslim, Ibn Mājah and al-Nasāʼī transmitted from Ibn ʻAbbās that he said: "Whoever prohibits his wife, it is nothing."

And (Ibn ʻAbbās) recited ﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah you have an excellent pattern﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 33:21]. In al-Nasāʼī it is reported that a man came to him and said, "I have made my wife unlawful to me," and he said: "You have lied; she is not unlawful to you," and then he recited this verse: ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾ [al-Taḥrīm 66:1]. The most severe expiation for him is freeing a slave, among other opinions. In this matter there are very many opinions, and there is also much disagreement in attributing the opinions to their proponents.

Whoever held that its dissolution is by expiation, if he does not make an exception, and who regarded the prohibition as absolute, or regarded the prohibition of a woman as an oath, uses this verse as evidence, because if it were not an oath, Allah would not have made expiation for an oath obligatory here.

It is answered: obligation of expiation does not necessarily imply that it is an oath, because two different matters may share one ruling; so expiation may be due in it for another reason. Even if it is granted that this expiation is only due with an oath, it is possible that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) swore along with the prohibition, saying about Māriyah, "By Allah, I will not have intercourse with her," or about the honey, "By Allah, I will not drink it." Some have reported this, so the expiation is for that oath, not for the prohibition alone. And Allah knows best.

﴿And Allah is your Mawlā⁠⁠ (protector and master)﴾: your sovereign and the one who manages your affairs. ﴿And He is the All-Knowing﴾, who knows what is good for you, so He legislates it for you, glory be to Him. ﴿The All-Wise﴾: the one who perfects His acts and rulings, so He commands you and forbids you only in accordance with what wisdom requires.

*"And when the Prophet confided to one of his wives a statement"* (﴿وإذْ أسَرَّ﴾): meaning, remember when the Prophet confided to one of his wives. She is Hafsa, according to what the majority of the exegetes hold. Some of the Shi'a claimed that she was 'A'isha, but no Shi'a group follows him in this. Ibn Mardawayh did narrate it from Ibn 'Abbas, but it is an anomalous (shadhdh) report. ﴿A statement﴾ (ḥadīthan) is his statement, upon him be prayers and peace, as in some narrations: "But I used to drink honey at the house of Zaynab bint Jahsh, so I will not return to it, and I have sworn. Do not tell anyone about this." ﴿Then when she told it﴾ means: informed (about it).

Talha read *anba'at* (she informed) ﴿with it﴾, meaning with the statement, to 'A'isha, because the two were close friends. The statement implied a loss of share for their co-wife Zaynab from their beloved, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, since he, upon him be prayers and peace, as in al-Bukhari and others, would stay with her for the drinking of that honey, and he had made this a habit, as the wording suggests: he used to... Hafsa was therefore carried away by joy and informed of it. ﴿And Allah made it known to him﴾ means: Allah made the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prevail over the statement, having learned of it, from the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿that He may make it prevail over all religion﴾ (al-Tawba 33; al-Fath 28; al-Saff 9). The expression, as it has been said, is figurative, or there is an elided noun, meaning: over its divulging. It has also been permitted that the pronoun refers to the verbal noun of ﴿informed﴾, though this involves the dislocation of pronouns (tafkik al-ḍamā'ir). Or Allah made the statement prevail over the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and this is like the expression "this matter became clear to me" and "it became clear upon me," when it involves additional effort and concern with the matter that has become clear. So do not be heedless.

﴿He made known﴾ (ʿarrafa): the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, made Hafsa know ﴿part of it﴾, that is, of the statement; he informed her and told her of part of the statement she had divulged.

The meaning is that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to her: "You said such-and-such," referring to some of what he had confided to her. It has been said that this was his saying to her: "I had drunk honey at the house of Zaynab bint Jahsh, so I will not return." ﴿And he turned away from part﴾: as it has been said, this was his statement, upon him be prayers and peace: "and I have sworn." He did not inform her of it, out of generosity, because of the additional embarrassment it would cause her, since it indicates his additional concern to please his wives, and he did not like this to spread. This is from the greatest of his generosity, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Ali, may Allah honour his face, that: "No noble man ever sought to scrutinize everything." Sufyan said: "Overlooking has always been a practice of the noble." The poet said:

*The fool is not a leader among his people,*
*but the leader of his people is the one who feigns ignorance.*

It has been permitted that ﴿ʿarrafa﴾ means *jāza* (to requite), i.e., he requited her for part of it with rebuke and blame, or by divorcing her, upon him be prayers and peace, and he overlooked part of it. This is supported by the recitation of al-Sulami, al-Hasan, Qatada, Talha, al-Kisa'i, and Abu 'Amr in the transmission of Harun from him, who read *'arafa* with a lightened pronunciation, because on this reading it cannot bear the meaning of knowledge, since knowledge was related to all of it, as is shown by the words "Allah made it known to him," while turning away from the remainder indicates knowledge. Therefore it is specified that it means requital.

Al-Azhari said in *al-Tahdhib*: "Whoever reads *'arafa* with a lightened pronunciation intends the meaning of being angry, and requites for it, as you say to a man who wrongs you: 'By Allah, I will surely make you know this.'" Al-Farra' approved of this. The statement of *al-Qamus* that it means *iqrar* (acknowledgment) has no basis here. The emphasized form was taken as an instance of mentioning the cause and wanting the effect, and the lightened form the reverse. It is also possible that the link between requital and making known is necessity (luzum).

The first meaning is supported by the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So when he informed her of it, she said: "Who told you this?" [to know whether 'A'isha had disgraced her or not]﴾. ﴿He said: "I was informed by the All-Knowing, the All-Aware"﴾, who nothing hidden escapes, for this is more suitable to informing. This is according to what is in *al-Bahr* (al-Bahr al-Muhit), in the sense of "by this."
