Ibn al-Musayyab and 'Ikrima read *'arrāfa ba'ḍahu* with an *alif* after the *rā'*, which is an elongation of the vowel. Ibn Khalawayh said: "It is said that it is a Yemeni dialect."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Abi Hatim from Mujahid, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, confided to Hafsa the prohibition of Mariya, and that Abu Bakr and 'Umar would govern the people after him. She divulged this to 'A'isha, so he made known to her part of it, namely the matter of Mariya, and turned away from part, namely that Abu Bakr and 'Umar would govern after him, out of fear that it would spread. It has also been said the reverse. The confiding of the matter of succession has come in several reports. Ibn 'Adi, Abu Nu'aym in *Fada'il al-Siddiq*, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated through a chain from 'Ali, may Allah honour his face, and from Ibn 'Abbas, who both said: "The leadership of Abu Bakr and 'Umar is in the Book of Allah: ﴿And when the Prophet confided to one of his wives a statement﴾. He said to Hafsa: 'Your father and the father of 'A'isha will govern the people after me, so beware of informing anyone.'"

Abu Nu'aym in *Fada'il al-Sahaba* narrated from al-Dahhak that he said about the verse: the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, confided to Hafsa that the successor after him would be Abu Bakr, and after Abu Bakr 'Umar. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated similarly from Maymun ibn Mihran. In *Majma' al-Bayan* by al-Tabarsi, from the most reliable of the Shi'a, from al-Zajjaj, he said: "When he, upon him be prayers and peace, prohibited Mariya the Copt, he informed her that Abu Bakr and 'Umar would rule after him. So he made known to her part of what she had divulged of the news and turned away from part, that Abu Bakr and 'Umar would rule after me." Something close to this is what al-‘Ayyashi narrated with a chain from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ata' al-Makki from Abu Ja'far al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with him, except that he added that each of them had told her father of it, so he rebuked them for the matter of Mariya and what they had divulged about it, and he turned away from rebuking them regarding the other matter. End of quotation.

If the Shi'a accept the soundness of this, it necessarily follows that they must affirm the soundness of the caliphate of the two Shaykhs, since it is manifest in it, as is not hidden. Furthermore, the interpretation of the verse according to these reports is clearer than its interpretation according to the hadith of the honey, but the hadith of the honey is more authentic, and reconciling the reports is hardly feasible.

The most that can be said: it is possible that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, drank honey at the house of Zaynab, as was his custom, then came to Hafsa and she said to him what she said, so he forbade honey. And it happened to him, upon him be prayers and peace, shortly before or after that, that he lay with his slave-girl Mariya in Hafsa's house on her day, on her bed, and she found out, so the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade Mariya, and said to Hafsa what he said to console her and asked her to keep it secret, but she divulged it, and what happened, happened. The verse was revealed after the two incidents, so some narrators confined themselves to one of them, and others to the other, and each said: "Then Allah revealed: ﴿O Prophet...﴾," etc. This is a true statement, since there is no claim by either that the cause of revelation is restricted to what he related. If this is established, the difference is minor; otherwise seek another explanation. And Allah knows best.

It has been derived from the verse that there is no harm in confiding part of a statement to one on whom one relies, whether a wife or a friend, and that it is obligatory for him to keep it secret. It is also said that the verse indicates that good conduct with wives is commendable, that gentleness in rebuke is good, and that turning away from pursuing the sin is good. It has been narrated that 'Abd Allah ibn Rawaha, one of the chieftains, had a slave-girl, and his wife accused him one night. He said something allusive, and she said: "If you did not approach her, then recite the Qur'an." So he recited:

*I testify, and I do not deny, that Muhammad*
*is the Messenger of He who is above the heavens on high,*

*and that Abu Yahya and Yahya, both of them,*
*have deeds in their religion that are accepted,*

*and that she who is in al-Jaza', from the belly of Nakhla,*
*and whoever follows her, each is removed from good.*

[Page 152]

She said: "Say more." So he recited:

*Among us is the Messenger of Allah reciting His Book,*
*as a known light shines bright from the dawn.*

*He brought guidance after blindness, so our souls*
*are certain by it that what he said will come to pass.*

*He keeps his side away from his bed*
*when the beds of the disbelievers are at rest.*

She said: "Say more." So he recited:

*I testify that the promise of Allah is true,*
*and that the Fire is the abode of the disbelievers.*

*And that Muhammad calls to truth,*
*and that Allah is the protector of the believers.*

*And that the Throne floats above the water,*
*and above the Throne is the Lord of the worlds.*

*And that it is carried by angels, strong,*
*the angels of God, marked out.*

She said: "As for you, since you have recited the Qur'an, I have believed you." In another narration, she said, having seen him in something she disliked: "Then Allah has spoken truly and my sight has lied." So he informed the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and he smiled and said: "The best of you is the best to his wives."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 66, verse 4:

﴿If you two turn in repentance to Allah﴾ is addressed to Hafsah and Aisha, may Allah be pleased with them both, and it is an iltifat (a shift in grammatical person, here from the third person to the second) for the sake of intensifying the reproach. For one who reproaches at length makes the one being reproached, at first, seem distant from the place of presence, and then, when his anger intensifies, he turns toward him and reproaches him with what he wishes. That the address is to both of them is based on what Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Hibban and others narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "I had not ceased being eager to ask Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) about the two wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning whom Allah the Exalted said: ﴿If you two turn in repentance﴾ and so on, until Umar performed the Hajj and I performed it with him. When we were on part of the road, Umar turned aside and I turned aside with him carrying the water-vessel. He relieved himself, then I poured water over his hands and he performed ablution. I said: 'O Commander of the Faithful, who are the two wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning whom Allah the Exalted said: ﴿If you two turn in repentance﴾ and so on?' He said: 'How strange you are, O son of Abbas! They are Aisha and Hafsah.' Then he began to narrate to me the hadith, the whole hadith at length."

As for the meaning of the words of the Exalted, ﴿for your hearts have inclined﴾: they have swerved from what is obligatory, in opposing him (ﷺ), by loving what he loves and disliking what he dislikes, toward opposing him. The clause stands in the place of the response of the conditional after its deletion, and the estimated sense is: "If you turn in repentance, then your repentance has a cause and a reason, ﴿for your hearts have inclined﴾," or "then it is due to you, for that which requires it has occurred," and it is in the sense of "it has become clear that this is the truth," as was said in his verse:

*"When we trace our lineage, a base woman did not bear me"*

with the meaning, by interpretation, "it has become clear that I was not borne by a base woman." Ibn al-Hajib (Ibn al-Hajib, the grammarian) made it a response in terms of informing, as was said in: "If you honour me today, I have honoured you yesterday." It was also said that the response is deleted, its estimate being: "He will erase your sin." His words, the Exalted, ﴿for your hearts have inclined﴾ and so on, explain the cause of repentance. It was also said that the estimate is: "You two have fulfilled what is incumbent upon you, or you have done what is due to you," and what has been mentioned is evidence for this. It was said: The reason they did not interpret ﴿your hearts have inclined﴾ as "inclined toward what is obligatory, or what is right, or what is good" is so that it may be correct to make it the response without needing something like what has preceded, because the form of the past tense with *qad* (قد), the reading of Ibn Masud (﴿your hearts have swerved﴾, فقد زاغت قلوبكما), and the abundance of meaning together with the brevity of wording require what has passed. It was objected that this only works according to the view of Ibn Malik that the response may be in the past tense even without the word *kana* (كان), and "there is room for consideration in this." The plural in ﴿your hearts﴾ rather than the dual is because of the disfavour of combining two duals when the intended meaning is clear, and in such a context the plural is more commonly used than the dual or the singular. Abu Hayyan said: "According to our companions, it is not permissible except in poetry," such as his verse:

*"O dove of the valley's two banks, sing!"*

Abu Hayyan, may Allah have mercy on him, also faulted Ibn Malik in his *al-Tashil*, where he said: "The singular form is preferred over the dual form."

﴿And if you two back each other against him﴾: with the deletion of one of the two *ta'*s and the lightening of the *za'* (ظاهرا, reading *tazahara*). This is the reading of Asim and, in one narration, Nafi', and of Talhah, al-Hasan and Abu Raja'. The majority, however, read *tazzaharā* with a shadda on the *za'*, its original form being *tatazaharā*, and the *ta'* was assimilated into the *za'*. Ikrimah read in accordance with the original form. Abu Amr, in another narration, read *tazzahharā* with shaddas on both the *za'* and the *ha'*, without an alif. The meaning is: "If you two cooperate against him (ﷺ) with what displeases him, through excessive jealousy and disclosing his secret."

﴿Then indeed Allah is his protector﴾, i.e., his helper. Stopping at what is mentioned in *al-Bahr* (Abu Hayyan's *al-Bahr al-Muhit*) and elsewhere here is better. They made the Exalted's words ﴿and Gabriel﴾ a subject (mubtada'), and His words, glorified is He, ﴿and the righteous among the believers and the angels﴾ are coordinated with it, and His words, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿after that﴾, i.e., after the help of Allah the Exalted, relate to His words, exalted is His majesty, ﴿are supporters﴾, and they made it the predicate for all of them, and it has the meaning of the plural, i.e., "backers." The singular was chosen because they are made like a single thing. It is also permitted that it be a predicate of "Gabriel," and its predicate is what follows it, which is estimated, like what they said in his verse:

*"And whoever's dwelling has become in Madina, then I and Qayyar are strangers there."*

It is also permitted that the stop be on "Gabriel," i.e., "and Gabriel is his protector, and the righteous among the believers" is a subject, and what follows it is coordinated with it, and the predicate is ﴿supporters﴾. The apparent sense of al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari's *al-Kashshaf*) is preference for stopping on "the believers," so that ﴿supporters﴾ is the predicate of the angels, and most of its abridgers follow this. The apparent sense of their statements is the estimation of a predicate for each of Gabriel and the righteous among the believers, and it is either the word *mawla* (مولى) used with each of its suitable meanings, i.e., "Gabriel is his *mawla*, i.e., his companion, and the righteous among the believers is his *mawla*, i.e., his follower," or another word with that suitable meaning, namely "companion" in the first and "follower" in the second. There is no obstacle to *mawla* in the plural meaning "helper," as is not hidden. The addition of ﴿He﴾ (هو) to what is in al-Kashshaf is to indicate that His help is one of His resolutions, and that He, Mighty and Majestic, is the one who undertakes that by His very essence, exalted is He. This is an explicit statement that the pronoun is not part of the separation (fasl) at all, and that it is for emphasis, not for restriction. Restriction is mostly found with the two definites (ma'rifatan), as transmitted in *al-Idah* (al-Farisi's *al-Idah*), although the speech of al-Sakkaki (al-Sakkaki) seems to imply obligation. This is so, and the emphasis is established, as stated by Sibawayh and verified in the *Usul* (Ibn al-Sarraj's *al-Usul*). As for restriction, it does not follow from the wording, so it is not objected that it would be better for ﴿and Gabriel﴾ and what follows it to be the subject of which "supporters" is the predicate. And even if that is granted, it does not conflict with it, because their support is His support, exalted is He, so there is nothing impossible in it, as in "Zayd is the one who departs, and Amr," as in al-Kashf (al-Taybi's *al-Kashf*). The reason for singling out Gabriel (peace be upon him) for mention is his great excellence; indeed he is the head of the cherubim (al-Karubiyyin). By "the righteous" (al-salih), according to most, is meant the genus, which includes few and many, and it is used here to mean the plural, like your saying: "I was among the nocturnal conversers (al-samir) and those present (al-hadir)." For this reason it is general by the construct (idafa). It is also permitted that the word be a collective, and the analogical form would be to write *wa-salihu* (وصالحو) with a *waw*, except that it was deleted in writing following its deletion in pronunciation. Some things in the codex (al-Mushaf) have been written following the pronunciation rather than the form of the script, such as ﴿and man prays for evil﴾ (al-Isra' 11), ﴿the caller calls﴾ (al-Qamar 6), ﴿We shall call the guards of hell﴾ (al-Alaq 18), and ﴿Has there come to you the news of the litigants?﴾ (Sad 21), and other examples. Some have held that the construct is for a specific reference (al-'ahd), so that it refers to the prophets (peace be upon them). It was transmitted from Ibn Zayd, Qatadah and al-Ala' ibn Ziyad, and that their support of him (ﷺ)... It was said: their words include condemnation of those who back up a prophet among the prophets (peace be upon them), but in this there is much obscurity. It was also said: it refers to Ali (may Allah ennoble his face), and Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Asakir narrated it from Ibn Abbas. Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Asma' bint Umays, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: ﴿and the righteous among the believers﴾ is Ali ibn Abi Talib." The Imamiyyah narrated from Abu Ja'far that when it was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) took the hand of Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) and said: "O people, this is the righteous among the believers."

Ibn Asakir narrated from al-Hasan al-Basri that he said: it is Umar ibn al-Khattab. He and a group narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: "﴿and the righteous among the believers﴾ was revealed concerning Umar ibn al-Khattab specifically." Ibn Asakir narrated from Muqatil ibn Sulayman that he said: "﴿and the righteous among the believers﴾ is Abu Bakr, Umar and Ali (may Allah be pleased with them)." It was also said: it is the four rightly-guided caliphs.

Al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat* and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Umar and Ibn Abbas, who both said: "﴿and the righteous among the believers﴾ was revealed concerning Abu Bakr and Umar." Ikrimah, Maymun ibn Mihran and others took its interpretation as referring to these two. Al-Hakim narrated from Abu Umamah, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in *Fada'il al-Sahabah* from Ibn Masud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "﴿and the righteous among the believers﴾ is Abu Bakr and Umar." Ibn Asakir narrated through the chain of al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "My father used to recite it: ﴿and the righteous among the believers﴾, Abu Bakr and Umar."

He (al-Alusi's source) preferred the intention of these two because it is most suitable for placing it between Gabriel and the angels (peace be upon them), for it combines the moral backing and the outward backing. How could it not be so, since Gabriel (peace be upon him) is a supporter of him (ﷺ), strengthening him with divine support, and these two are his ministers and supporters in managing the affairs of the message and carrying out its apparent rulings? Moreover, the explanation of their backing of him (peace be upon him) has a stronger effect on the hearts of their two daughters and weakens their cause.

I say: generality is preferable. These two, and likewise Ali (may Allah ennoble his face), enter it by primary inclusion. Specifying some individuals in the raised (marfu') reports, if they are sound, is for a purpose requiring that, not to intend restriction. This is supported by what Ibn Asakir narrated from Ibn Masud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said about it: "Among the righteous of the believers are Abu Bakr and Umar."

The benefit of ﴿after that﴾ is to draw attention to the fact that the help of the angels (peace be upon them) is the strongest aspect of His help, Mighty and Majestic is He, although its kinds vary. Then there is no doubt that the help of all the angels, among whom is Gabriel, is stronger than the help of Gabriel (peace be upon him) alone.

It was said: the reference is to the backing of the righteous among the believers specifically, so the magnification is relative to them. In drawing attention to this is the removal of the imagined notion suggested by the sequence of mention, namely that the backing of the one mentioned first is greater. In sum, the benefit of ﴿after that﴾ is like the benefit of "thumma" (then) in His words: ﴿then he was among those who believed﴾ (al-Balad 17), namely the gradation of rank, i.e., the greater rank of what comes after relative to what comes before. This does not hold according to what is transmitted from *al-Bahr*. Rather, it is to indicate that those mentioned follow in the help and assistance of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Whatever the case, the conditional clause ﴿and if you two back each other﴾ is the protasis (fi'l al-shart), and the sentence joined with *fa* (then) is the indication of the response, and it is a cause placed in its stead. The original is: "then He will not leave without help whoever backs him, for Allah is his protector." It is also permitted that the sentence itself is the response, on the basis that it is metaphorical or a metonymy for that. He (Allah) magnified the matter of help for His Prophet (ﷺ) over these two weak women, either to indicate the great deceit of women, or to intensify the cutting of the ropes of their hope, because of their great station with the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) and with the believers, and because they are their mothers, and out of honour for him (ﷺ) and consideration for their two parents, in that their backing would benefit them.

It was also said: the purpose is to intensify the weakening of the matter of their backing and to repel what the hypocrites might imagine of harm from it, in the matter of prophethood, conveying the message, and subduing the enemies of the religion. For custom dictates that a man's mind is occupied by the backing of his wives against him. In this there is also further enraging of the hypocrites and cutting off of their vain hopes. It is as if it were said: "If they back each other against him, that does not harm his affair, for Allah the Exalted is his protector and helper in the matter of his religion and all his affairs, against everyone who confronts what he dislikes." ﴿And Gabriel and the righteous among the believers and the angels after that﴾ are supporters of him and helpers to him likewise. This harmonizes with the omission of mention of the one helped against him, where He did not say "a supporter of him against you two," for example, and likewise the omission of mention of the one helped in it, and the singling out of "the righteous among the believers" for mention. This harmony is strengthened according to what is transmitted from Ibn Jubayr, who interpreted "the righteous among the believers" as the one who is free of hypocrisy. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 66, verse 5:

﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him in exchange wives better than you﴾ That is, He will give him, peace and blessings be upon him, in place of you, ﴿wives better than you﴾. The address is to all of the wives of the Prophet, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, who are the Mothers of the Believers, by way of iltifat (a shift from direct address to third person and back). They were addressed because they were at the place of the descent of revelation and the arena of honour and presence. What points to this is what al-Bukhari transmitted from Anas, who said: Umar said: "The wives of the Prophet, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, banded together in jealousy against him, so I said: ‘It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him in exchange wives better than you,’" and then this verse was revealed. It does not state that he, peace be upon him, did not divorce Hafsah, nor that there are among women others better than them. However, the prevailing view, as has been said, is that there is no one on the face of the earth better than them, because suspending the divorce of all of them does not contradict divorcing one of them, and what is conditional on something that has not occurred does not necessarily occur. It is also permissible that the address be to all of them by way of taghlib (predominance of the masculine/majority form), while the original address was to two of them, who were the ones addressed first by the words of the Exalted: ﴿If you two turn in repentance to Allah, your hearts have certainly inclined﴾, etc. So it is as if it were said: "It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you two and others besides you, will give him in exchange wives better than you two and better than others among wives." The apparent meaning is that the non-indication of the verse that he, peace be upon him, did not divorce Hafsah, and that among women there are others better than the wives of the Prophet, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, remains as it is, because the conditional is upon the divorce of two, which did not occur, so what is conditional does not necessarily occur, and it does not contradict divorcing one. Al-Khafaji said: there is taghlib in addressing all, although the first addressed were two, and also in the conditional particle "in" which indicates the non-occurrence of divorce.

It has been narrated that he, peace be upon him, did divorce Hafsah, so what did not occur of divorce was given predominance over what did occur. And if it is generalized, there is no taghlib in the address nor in "in." End of quotation. There is discussion in this. Then, the well-known view is that ﴿عَسى﴾ (ʿasā, "it may be") in the speech of the Exalted is for obligation (wujub), and that the obligation here is only after the condition is fulfilled. It has been said that it is so in all cases except here, and that the condition is interposed between the subject of ʿasā and its predicate.

The answer (jawab) is omitted, meaning: "if he divorces you, then ʿasā..." etc. ﴿أزْواجًا﴾ (azwājan, "wives") is the second object of yubdila (to give in exchange), ﴿خَيْرًا﴾ (khayran, "better") is its adjective, and likewise what follows. Abu ʿAmr, in the narration of ʿAyyash, read "ṭallaqakkunna" with the qaf assimilated into the kaf.

Nafi', Abu ʿAmr and Ibn Kathir read "yubaddilahu" with the doubling (shaddah) for intensification (li-l-takthir). ﴿مُسْلِماتٍ﴾ (muslimāt, "submissive") meaning those who acknowledge; ﴿مُؤْمِناتٍ﴾ (mu'minat, "faithful") meaning sincere, because belief requires the assent of the heart, and that is only sincere; or meaning those who submit, since islam in its linguistic sense is also taṣdīq (affirmation). ﴿قانِتاتٍ﴾ (qanitat, "devout") meaning those who pray, or those who are constant in obedience absolutely. ﴿تائِباتٍ﴾ (ta'ibat, "repentant") meaning those who abandon sin. ﴿عابِداتٍ﴾ (ʿabidat, "worshipful") meaning those who worship, or who humble themselves to the command of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace. ﴿سائِحاتٍ﴾ (sa'ihat, "fasting") meaning fasting, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Hurayrah, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, Zayd ibn Aslam and his son ʿAbd al-Rahman, and it is narrated from the Prophet, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace. Al-Farra' said: the fasting person is called sa'ih because the wanderer (sa'ih) has no provision with him, and he eats wherever he finds food. It is narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam and Yaman: "emigrating" (muhajirat). Ibn Zayd said: there is no sia-hah (wandering) in Islam except hijrah. It has also been said: "going forth in obedience to Allah, the Exalted, in whatever direction."

ʿAmr ibn Fa'id read "sayyihat." ﴿ثَيِّباتٍ﴾ (thayyibat, "previously married") is the plural of thayyib, from thaba yathubu thawban; its pattern is fayyal like sayyid, and it refers to she who returns (tathubu) from the husband, meaning after the loss of her virginity. ﴿وأبْكارًا﴾ (abkaran, "virgins") is the plural of bikr, from bakara, when one goes out at the beginning of the day (bukrah), which is the first part of the day; there is in it the sense of precedence, and the virgin was so named because she has not been deflowered, in contrast to the thayyib, because she precedes her in what women are desired for. The conjunction was omitted among the preceding attributes because they are attributes that gather in one thing and between them there is a strong connection which requires omitting the conjunction. The conjunction was inserted here to indicate the difference of the two attributes and that they do not come together in one entity. "Aw" (or) was not used; it has been said: so that the meaning would be "wives, some of whom are thayyibat and some of whom are abkar." Close to this is what was said: the conjunction was placed between the two attributes because they are in the ruling of one attribute, since the meaning is inclusive of the thayyibat and the abkar, so reflect. In al-Insaf of Ibn al-Munir: Shaykh Ibn al-Hajib mentioned to me that the judge al-Fadil ʿAbd al-Rahim al-Bisani, the secretary, used to believe that the waw in the verse is the waw which some weak grammarians called "the waw of eight," because it was mentioned with the eighth attribute. Al-Fadil used to boast of extracting it beyond the three well-known places before it: one in al-Tawbah, ﴿the repentant, the worshippers﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and those who forbid evil﴾ [9:112]; the second in His saying: ﴿and their eighth is their dog﴾ [18:22]; the third in His saying: ﴿and its gates shall be opened﴾ [39:73]. Until one day he mentioned this in the presence of Abu al-Jud the grammarian and reciter, who showed him that he was mistaken in counting it among that category, and referred to the meaning given by al-Zamakhshari about the necessity that drives to bringing it here, since two attributes cannot be combined in one described subject; and the waw of eight, if it is established, occurs only where there is no need for it, except to indicate the completion of the final limit of the number, which is seven. Al-Fadil acknowledged this and admired it from him, and said: "You have guided us, O Abu al-Jud." End of quotation.

The two kinds are mentioned because among the wives of the Prophet, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, there are those he married as thayyibat and among them those he married as virgins. It is reported that he, peace be upon him, did not marry a virgin except ʿA'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, and she used to boast of that over her co-wives. Al-Zahra' (Fatimah), upon her father and upon her be peace, answered her by the teaching of the Prophet, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, to her when she boasted over her mother Khadijah, may Allah be pleased with her, by her saying: "My mother was married by the Messenger of Allah, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, while he was a virgin whom no woman had seen except her, and it is not so with you," and she (ʿA'ishah) was silent.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 66, verse 6:

﴿O you who have believed, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire﴾ — nāran, i.e., a kind of fire — ﴿whose fuel is people and stones﴾. It is kindled by them as other fires are kindled by firewood. The protection of oneself from the Fire is by abandoning sins and performing acts of obedience. The protection of the family is by bringing them to that through counsel and discipline. It is narrated that when this verse was revealed, ʿUmar said: "O Messenger of Allah, we protect ourselves, so how can we protect our families?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You forbid them from what Allah has forbidden you and command them to do what Allah has commanded you, and that will be a protection between them and the Fire."

Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, along with a group of others, narrated from ʿAli (may Allah ennoble his face) that he said concerning the verse: "Teach yourselves and your families good and discipline them." By "the family" is meant, as has been said, what includes the wife, the child, the male slave and the female slave.

It has been used as evidence that a man is obliged to learn the obligatory duties (farāʾiḍ) and to teach them to these people. Some scholars included children among "the selves," since the child is a part of his father. In a hadith: "May Allah have mercy on a man who says: O my family, your prayer, your fasting, your zakat, your dwelling, your orphan, your neighbours. Perhaps Allah will gather you with Him in Paradise." It has also been said that the most severely punished people on the Day of Resurrection are those who were ignorant of their families.

It is read as wa-ahlūkum with a wāw, and this is a conjunction upon the pronoun in ﴿qū﴾, and the conjunction is good because of the separation by the object. The estimate according to some is: "and let your families protect their selves." Al-Zamakhshari did not accept this, and he mentioned what amounts to: the original is ﴿qū﴾ — you and your families — "your selves and their selves," that each of you and of them protects and guards his own self from what destroys it. So he put "your selves" first, and made the pronoun attached to "the selves" include the family by way of predominance (taghlīb), so that the address included them. Likewise predominance is considered in ﴿qū﴾. In this there is a reduction of deletion and a preference for the single conjunction, which is the original, and the predominance whose purpose is to indicate primacy and subordination.

Al-Hasan and Mujahid read wuqūduhā with a ḍamma on the wāw, meaning: having its fuel. The full discussion of this verse is known from what passed in Surat al-Baqara. ﴿Over it are angels﴾, meaning they are appointed over it, managing its affairs and the punishment of its people, and they are the nineteen Guardians (al-Zabāniyya). It is said: and their helpers. ﴿Harsh and severe﴾: harsh in speech, severe in deeds; or harsh in character, severe in creation, strong in severe acts. ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad narrated in Zawāʾid al-Zuhd from Abu ʿImran al-Jawni, who said: "We have been told that the guardians of the Fire are nineteen, the distance between the shoulders of one of them being a hundred years' journey, having no mercy in their hearts; they were created only for punishment. An angel strikes a man of the people of the Fire with one blow, leaving him crushed from his horn to his foot."

﴿They do not disobey Allah in what He commands them﴾ — this is another attribute of the angels, and "mā" is in the accusative position as a substitute: they do not disobey what Allah commands, as in His saying: ﴿Did you disobey my command?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 93]; or with the preposition dropped: they do not disobey in what He commands them. ﴿And they do what they are commanded﴾, i.e., what the Mighty and Majestic commands them. The first clause negates opposition and arrogance on their part, peace be upon them, as in His saying: ﴿They do not disdain from His worship﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 206]. The second establishes their diligence and negates laziness in them, as in His saying: ﴿Nor do they tire﴾ up to ﴿they do not slacken﴾ [al-Anbiya: 19–20]. In other words, the first indicates acceptance inwardly, for disobedience at its root means refusal and rejection, and disobedience of a command is by its reality a quality of the inner self, since performing what is commanded counts as obedience only when done with the intention of compliance. So the negation of disobedience from them shows their acceptance and their not refusing inwardly. The second is for carrying out what is commanded without sluggishness or laxity, as indicated by the continuity derived from "yafʿalūna." There is no repetition. As for the attainment of "they do not disobey," it refers to the past, and the present tense is used to narrate a past state; "and they do what they are commanded" refers to the future.

It is also permitted that this is of the type of ṭard and ʿaks, which is every pair of statements where the first establishes by its explicit meaning the implied sense of the second, and vice versa, as an intensification in that they are not taken by compassion in executing the commands of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and in being zealous for Him, glorified be He.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 66, verse 7:

﴿O you who have disbelieved, do not make excuses today﴾ is a speech (maqul) to a statement that has been omitted, relying on the context (dalalat al-hal) to indicate it. It is said to them this when the angels bring them into the Fire, in accordance with what they were commanded. So the definite article in "today" (al-yawm) is for a known reference (al-'ahd), and the prohibition against them making excuses is because they have no excuse, or because an excuse will not benefit them. ﴿You are only being recompensed for what you used to do﴾ in the worldly life, of disbelief and sins, after you were forbidden from them in the strongest terms and commanded to believe and obey in the most complete manner.

[Page 158]

﴿O you who believe, turn in repentance to God﴾ from sins.

﴿a sincere repentance﴾ meaning one that is exceedingly sincere (nuṣḥ). It is of the intensive form (mubālagha), like ḍurūb (very much striking). Repentance is described by it through metaphorical attribution (al-isnād al-majāzī), which is the attribution of the description to the penitents. It means that they give sincere advice to their own souls, so they come to repentance in its proper way. Perhaps this is what is contained in what Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "Muʿādh ibn Jabal said: O Messenger of God, what is sincere repentance? He said: That the servant regrets the sin he committed, then seeks forgiveness from God Most High, then does not return to it, just as milk does not return to the udder." Its explanation has also been narrated in this sense from ʿUmar, Ibn Masʿūd, Ubayy, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid and others.

It has also been said: nuṣūḥan derives from nuṣāḥat al-thawb, meaning its stitching, i.e., a repentance that mends your breaches in your religion and fills your gaps. It has also been said: it means pure, from their saying "ʿasal nāṣiḥ" (pure honey) when it is free of wax. It is also permissible that it means a repentance that gives advice to people, i.e., that calls them to its like, because its effect is evident in the one who repents, and in the use of earnestness and resolve in acting upon its requirements. Regarding its meaning there are many sayings; some have brought them to more than twenty, among them what you have heard.

Zayd ibn ʿAlī read tawban (without the tā' of the feminine). al-Ḥasan, al-Aʿraj, ʿĪsā, Abū Bakr (from ʿĀṣim) and Khārija (from Nāfiʿ) read nuṣūḥan with a ḍamma on the nūn. It is the verbal noun of naṣaḥa, for al-nuṣḥ and al-naṣūḥ are like al-shukr and al-shakūr, and al-kufr and al-kafūr. That is: possessing sincerity (dhāt nuṣḥ), or "they give sincere advice" (tanṣaḥu nuṣūḥan), or "turn in repentance for the sake of advising your souls," with it being a verbal object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu).

That said, discussion of repentance is extensive. Since it is the most important of the Islamic commands, the first of the spiritual stations, the starting point of the path of the wayfarers, and the key to the door of those who arrive, there is no harm in mentioning some of what relates to it. So we say: linguistically it is "return" (rujūʿ). Legally, as a description of us, according to what al-Saʿd said, it is regret over disobedience because it is disobedience. For regret over it because it harms the body, or spoils honour or wealth, for example, is not repentance. As for regret out of fear of Hell or desire for Paradise, there is hesitation about whether it is repentance. The matter rests on whether such regret is regret over the sin because of its ugliness and because it is disobedience, or not. Likewise, regret over it because of its ugliness together with another purpose. The truth is that if the aspect of ugliness is such that, were it to stand alone, regret would be realized, then it is repentance; otherwise not, as when the purpose is the combination of both matters and not each one of them separately. The same applies to repentance at a fatal illness, based on whether that regret is due to the ugliness of the sin or merely out of fear. The apparent sense of the reports is that repentance is accepted as long as the signs of death have not appeared and its arrival is not realized in the customary way.

The meaning of regret is grief and anguish over having done it, and wishing that one had not done it. This is necessary, for it is certain that mere abstention, like a debauched person who tires of his debauchery and then turns to some permissible things, is not repentance. Also, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Regret is repentance." Sometimes the condition of firm resolve not to return to its like is added.

It has been objected that committing the sin in the future may not occur to one's mind because of heedlessness, madness or the like, and one may not be able to commit it due to a hindrance such as muteness in the case of slander, or castration in the case of fornication. Then the resolve to abstain cannot be conceived, because it implies power and choice.

It has been answered that what is meant is resolve to abstain on the assumption that the thought occurs and one has the ability, so that even if the ability is taken away, resolve to abstain is not a condition. This is what the words of Imam al-Ḥaramayn (al-Juwaynī) suggest, where he said: "The resolve not to return is only joined with repentance in some states and is not constant in every state, for resolve is valid only from one who is able to do the like of what he did before. The castrated person cannot validly resolve to abstain from fornication, nor can the mute person resolve to abstain from slander." Some eminent scholars said: "The verification is that the mention of resolve is for clarification and affirmation, not for restriction and exclusion, for the one who regrets the sin because of its ugliness is never free of that resolve, on the assumption that the thought occurs and he is able." The sign of regret is prolonged sorrow, fear, and the flowing of tears. Among the strange things reported is that a sign of true regret for a sin like fornication is that one does not see in a dream that he is doing it by choice, for that suggests the persistence of his love for it and that its roots have not been wholly uprooted from his heart, which contradicts sincere regret.

The Muʿtazila (a rationalist school) said: repentance suffices if one believes that he did wrong and that, if it were possible for him to undo that disobedience, he would undo it. There is no need for sorrow and grief, since that leads to imposing what cannot be borne.

Imam al-Nawawī said: "Repentance is not complete unless it combines three matters: that one ceases the disobedience, regrets doing it, and resolves firmly never to return to its like. If the sin concerns another human being, it is obligatory to return the wrong to its owner or his heir, or to obtain his pardon. Its greatest pillar is regret."

In Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid they said: "If the disobedience is purely the right of God Most High, then regret may suffice, as in fleeing from battle or abandoning enjoining good. Sometimes it requires an additional matter, such as surrendering oneself to the prescribed punishment for drinking, and surrendering what is due for abandoning zakat, and similarly for abandoning prayer. If it concerns the rights of servants, then along with regret and resolve it is obligatory to deliver the servant's right or its substitute to him, if the sin was oppression, as in usurpation or deliberate killing. It is obligatory to guide him if the sin was leading him astray, and to apologise to him if it was harm, as in backbiting when it reaches him. It is not obligatory to detail what one backbit him with, unless it reached him in a more abominable form." The verification is that this additional requirement is a separate obligation outside repentance, according to what Imam al-Ḥaramayn said: if a killer regrets without surrendering himself to retaliation, his repentance is valid as regards the right of God Most High, but his refusal of retaliation from the one entitled to it is a renewed disobedience requiring repentance, and this does not invalidate repentance from killing. He then said: "Sometimes repentance is not valid without release from the servant's right, as in usurpation. So there is a difference between killing and usurpation, and its reason is not hidden from the reflective."

The people of the Sunna and others have not disagreed that repentance is obligatory for the committers of major sins. They differed regarding the proof. For us it is revelation (samʿ), like this verse and others, and the command in them is taken to be a concession and an announcement of its acceptance, and to dispel despair, as al-Āmidī permitted as a possibility. Building on this, the non-reward for it is hardly acceptable. According to the Muʿtazila it is reason (ʿaql). The Jahmiyya (an early theological sect) made repentance from minor sins obligatory by revelation, not by reason, and the people of the Sunna agree with this. The implication of the words of al-Nawawī, al-Māzarī and others is that it is obligatory at the time of being engaged in the sin. The words of al-Māzarī are: "They agreed that repentance from all sins is obligatory, that it is obligatory immediately, and that it is not permissible to delay it, whether the sin was minor or major."

In Sharḥ al-Jawhara: continuing in a sin by delaying repentance from it is one disobedience, as long as one does not intend to repeat it. The Muʿtazila explicitly said that it is obligatory immediately, so that delaying it for an hour incurs another sin, from which repentance is obligatory, two hours incurs two sins, and so on. Indeed, they mentioned that delaying repentance from a major sin by one hour gives one two major sins: the disobedience and the abandonment of repentance; two hours gives four: the first two and the abandonment of repentance for each of them; three hours gives eight, and so on. Repentance may be valid from one sin and not from another, because regret and resolve not to return are realised. Abū Hāshim disagreed, arguing that regret over disobedience must be for its ugliness, and this covers all of them, so regret for one ugly act is not realised while persisting in another.

It has been answered that what covers all is the ugliness itself, not the specific ugliness of that particular disobedience. This disagreement concerns other than the unbeliever who becomes Muslim and repents from his unbelief while still persisting in some sins. As for him, his repentance is valid and his Islam likewise, by consensus, and he is punished only with the punishment of that sin. Yes, it is disputed whether his mere faith counts as repentance, or whether regret over his past unbelief is required. According to the majority, his mere faith is repentance. Al-Imam (al-Juwaynī) and al-Qurṭubī said: regret over past unbelief is required. That righteous deeds are not a condition is agreed upon by the leading scholars, against Ibn Ḥazm. Likewise, repentance from sins may be valid in general without specifying what one repents from, even if specifying it were not difficult for him. Some Mālikīs disagreed and said: it is valid in general only for what is known in general; but for what is known in detail, repentance from it must be in detail. A legitimate repentance is not annulled by relapse, so his past sins do not return to him. Rather, the relapse and the breaking of repentance is another disobedience, from which he must repent.

The Muʿtazila said: one of the conditions of its validity is that one does not return to the sin. If one returns to it, his repentance is annulled and his sins return, because the regret required in it is realised only through continuity. The Qāḍī Abū Bakr and the majority agreed with them that continuing regret is not obligatory; rather the condition is that nothing arises that contradicts and dispels it, because then it is effectively continuous, like faith during sleep. Requiring continuity entails excessive hardship. al-Āmidī said: it also entails the invalidity of prayers and all other acts of worship, and it entails that, on the assumption of not continuing regret and not recalling it, one is not a penitent, and that it becomes obligatory on him to repeat repentance, which is contrary to consensus.

Yes, the scholars differed about one who recalls the sin after repenting from it: is it obligatory for him to renew regret? The Qāḍī among us went to this, as did Abū ʿAlī of the Muʿtazila, on the claim that if he did not regret every time he recalled it, he would be desiring it and rejoicing in it, and that would nullify regret and amount to a return to persistence. The answer is denial, since he may turn away from it without regret or desire for it and without delight in it. Were the matter as stated, the earlier repentance would not be valid. The Qāḍī himself said: if he does not renew regret, that is a new disobedience requiring regret, while the first repentance remains valid, because a past act of worship is not nullified by anything after it has been established. End.

Imam al-Ḥaramayn explicitly stated that renewal is not obligatory on recalling the sin. From their words it is understood that the disagreement applies when he does not take delight in the sin on recalling or hearing it, does not rejoice, and does not relish its mention. Otherwise renewal is obligatory by agreement. The apparent sense of their words is that relapse does not invalidate repentance even if it happens in the session of repentance, and even if it is repeated in a way that amounts to trifling. On this last point there is room for consideration, for al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ said: "One who commits, against the right of God Most High, what is unbelief, his repentance benefits him despite severe punishment, so that this may be a deterrent for him and for those like him. But if this is repeated by him, and his contempt for what he did is known, then this is evidence of a corrupt inner disposition and a false repentance." End.

"Sincere repentance" ought to be qualified so that the sins are not committed so frequently that they show contempt and bring the one who commits them to the border of madness. Scholars have differed over whether a temporary repentance is valid, one made without persistence in sin, such as refraining from sins or from a particular sin for a certain number of years. Some said it is valid and others said it is not. In the commentary on *al-Jawhara*, the analogy is drawn that its validity for some sins but not others is comparable to its validity in what has been mentioned.

Repentance (*tawbah*) has degrees. The highest of them is what is reported from Ya'subu al-Mu'minin (the chief of the believers), may Allah ennoble his face, that he heard a Bedouin say, "O Allah, I seek Your forgiveness and I repent to You." He said, "O man, quickness of the tongue in repentance is the repentance of liars." The Bedouin said, "What is repentance?" He, may Allah ennoble his face, said, "It comprises six things: regret for the sins of the past; restoring the obligatory acts (by making them up); returning what was taken unjustly; seeking the pardon of those wronged; resolving never to return to them; and making yourself melt in obedience to Allah as you had nurtured it in disobedience, and making it taste the bitterness of obedience as you made it taste the sweetness of sins."

By restoring the obligatory acts is meant making up those that were missed during the time of disobedience. For example, a drinker of wine repeats his prayer before repentance, because it was generally contaminated by impurity. This is a repentance of the elite (*khawass*), so there is no basis for this report in the view of Ibn Hazm and his like, as is not hidden.

Then Allah, exalted is He, explained the benefit of repentance by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Perhaps your Lord will remove from you your misdeeds and admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. It has been said that the meaning is that He, mighty and majestic, does this, but the expression of hope (*"'asa"*) is used following the custom of kings, for when they intend an act they say, "Perhaps we will do such-and-such." It also indicates that this is a bounty from Him, glorified is He, and that repentance does not oblige Him to do it.

It is also the case that the servant should be between fear and hope, even if he strives greatly in the performance of the duties of worship.

The verse has been used as evidence that accepting repentance is not obligatory, because the expiation of sins is the result of acceptance, and it is expressed with the language of hope rather than certainty. This question is disputed. The Mu'tazilah held that it is obligatory upon Allah, exalted is He, to accept it by reason, and they put forward ornate premises in this regard. Imam al-Haramayn and al-Qadi Abu Bakr said: it is obligatory to accept it by revelation and promise, but on the basis of a probable (*zanni*) proof, since no decisive text that does not admit of interpretation has been established on this matter. Shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari said: rather, it is on the basis of a decisive (*qat'i*) proof. The point of dispute between al-Ash'ari and his two students concerns everything other than the repentance of the disbeliever. As for the latter, there is consensus on its acceptance with certainty, by revelation, because there is an unanimously transmitted (*mutawatir*) text to that effect, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they desist, what has passed will be forgiven for them﴾ [al-Anfal: 38]. This is unlike what has come concerning the repentance of others, which is only apparent, and it is not a definitive text regarding the forgiveness of the sins of a Muslim through repentance, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾ [az-Zumar: 53]. As for the hadith "Repentance erases what came before it," it is not unanimously transmitted. Moreover, if the acceptance of the disbeliever's repentance is held with certainty, that opens the door to faith and leads to it, and if the acceptance of a believer's repentance is not held with certainty, that closes the door to disobedience and prevents it. This and what preceded it were mentioned by the judge (al-Qadi) when it was said to him that the proofs were on the side of Shaykh Abu al-Hasan.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the majority of the People of the Sunnah hold the view of the judge. The evidence for this is that every repentant person supplicates for the acceptance of his repentance, and if it were certain, supplication would have no meaning. Similarly, the obligation of gratitude for acceptance: if it were obligatory, gratitude for it would not be obligatory.

Al-Sa'd objected to this, saying that it may be answered that what is asked for in the supplication is that the person gather the conditions of acceptance, for the matter is grave. And the obligation of acceptance does not contradict the obligation of gratitude, since it is a favour in itself, like a parent raising his child.

Imam al-Nawawi said: according to the People of the Sunnah, it is not obligatory upon Allah, exalted is He, to accept repentance when it is made with its conditions, but He, glorified is He, accepts it out of generosity and bounty. We know its acceptance by the Sharia and by consensus, so do not be heedless.

It was recited as ﴿yudkhilkum﴾ with the *lam* vowelled with sukun, and Abu Hayyan explained it as the dropping of the vowel for lightness, treating what is in two words as a single word, since it is said *qam'in* as *qam'in* and *nat'in* as *nat'in*. He said this is preferable to its being for coordination with the position (*mahall*) of ﴿perhaps your Lord will remove﴾. Al-Zamakhshari chose this, as if it were said: "Repent, so that expiation may be hoped for, or it obliges the expiation of your misdeeds and admits you ﴿on the day when Allah will not disgrace the Prophet﴾." The phrase "on the day" is an adverbial of time governed by ﴿will admit you﴾. The definiteness of "the Prophet" is definite by prior reference, and what is meant is the master of the prophets, Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. What is meant by negating disgrace is affirming all kinds of honour and dignity.

In al-Qamus it is said: "Allah disgraced so-and-so" means He exposed him. Al-Raghib said: it is said "the man was disgraced" when he is overtaken by humiliation, either from himself, which is excessive shame, and its verbal noun is *khaza'ah*; or from others, which is a kind of belittling, and its verbal noun is *khizy*. ﴿The day when Allah will not disgrace the Prophet﴾ is closer to the second meaning, and it may be that it includes both together. ﴿And those who believed with him﴾ is coordinated with him (the Prophet), upon whom be blessings and peace. In this there is an allusion to those whom Allah disgraced from among the people of disbelief and wickedness, and a praise for the believers that He preserved them from a situation like theirs. The word "faith" here means its complete instance, as mentioned by al-Khafaji. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Their light runs before them and on their right﴾, meaning on the Path (*sirat*), as has been said. The discussion of it has passed as a separate sentence, and likewise His saying, glorified is He: ﴿They say﴾ and so on. It has been allowed that the two sentences are in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to the relative pronoun; that the first is a circumstantial clause relating to it and the second a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun in ﴿runs﴾; that the first is a new sentence and the second relates to the pronoun; that the first is a circumstantial clause relating to the relative pronoun and the second a new sentence; or that the first is a circumstantial clause relating to the relative and the second is a new sentence or a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun. It has also been allowed that the relative pronoun is the subject, its predicate being "with him," and the two sentences are further predicates, or new sentences, or circumstantial clauses relating to the relative pronoun, or the first is a circumstantial clause relating to it and the second a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun, or the first is a new sentence and the second a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun, or the first is a circumstantial clause and the second a new sentence, or the first is a predicate after a predicate and the second is a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun or a new sentence. It has also been allowed that the relative pronoun is the subject whose predicate is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Their light runs﴾ and so on, with the other sentence being a new sentence, or a circumstantial clause, or a predicate after a predicate. These are a number of possibilities, and it is not hidden which of them is most apparent.

According to what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan, the saying will occur when the light of the hypocrites is extinguished, meaning: they will say when the light of the hypocrites is extinguished, ﴿Our Lord, perfect for us our light and forgive us; indeed You are over all things competent﴾. In another report from al-Hasan, they supplicate, drawing near to Allah, exalted is He, while their light is complete. It has also been said that this is said by one who passes over the Path crawling and creeping.

This part is completed from another copy. It has also been said: one is given light in proportion to what he needs to see the place of his foot. It is known from this that the restriction of the meaning of faith to its complete instance is not binding, as you heard from al-Khafaji.

Sahl ibn Shu'ayb al-Sahmi and Abu Haywa recited ﴿wa-bi-iymanihim﴾ with a kasra on the hamza, as a verbal noun coordinated with the adverbial of place, meaning: being between their hands, and being by means of their faith.

﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers﴾ with the sword, ﴿and the hypocrites﴾ with argument, ﴿and be harsh with them﴾. Employ harshness toward both groups in whatever you strive against them with, when gentleness has reached its limit.

From al-Hasan (al-Basri): most of the hudud (prescribed punishments) in that era fell upon the hypocrites, so the Prophet, upon him be peace, was commanded to be strict with them in enforcing the hudud.

Al-Tabarsi (Abu 'Ali al-Fadl ibn al-Hasan al-Tabarsi, author of Majma' al-Bayan) reports from al-Baqir (Muhammad al-Baqir) that he recited: "Strive against the disbelievers with the hypocrites." I think this is a lie of the Imamiyyah (the Twelver Shi'a), may Allah deal with them according to His justice. ﴿Their abode is Hell﴾, meaning they will there suffer a severe punishment. ﴿And wretched is the destination﴾, meaning Hell, or their abode. The conjunction (al-'atf) has been said to be the linking of one narrative (qissah) to another narrative.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 66, verse 10:**

﴿Allah sets forth an example for those who disbelieve.﴾ *Darb al-mathal* (setting forth a parable or example) in a context like this means presenting a strange situation so that another situation, similar to it in strangeness, may be known through it. That is, Allah, exalted is He, made the condition and the outcome of the disbelievers an example, with *mathalan* being the second object of *daraba*, and the *lam* being attached to it.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿the wife of Noah﴾, whose name is said to be Wali'ah, ﴿and the wife of Lot﴾, whose name is said to be Wahilah, or said to be Wahilah... and it is related from Muqatil that the name of Noah's wife was Wali'ah, and the name of Lot's wife was Wahilah, is its first object. It was placed after it so that what explains and clarifies their condition would be connected to it, and the condition of the disbelievers becomes clear through this. The meaning is: Allah, exalted is He, set forth an example for the condition of those people, the condition of ﴿the wife﴾ and so on. So His saying, exalted is He, ﴿they were under two of Our righteous servants﴾ is an explanation of their condition, which called them to good and righteousness. He did not say *tahtahuma* (under them), for glorification, meaning: they were in the marriage of two prophets of great standing, able to attain the good of this world and the Hereafter and to obtain their happiness.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿but they betrayed them﴾ is an explanation of the great betrayal that issued from them, despite the presence of what would preclude it, namely accompanying the Prophet (ﷺ). As for the betrayal of Noah's wife, she used to tell the people that he was mad. As for the betrayal of Lot's wife, she used to point out the guests. This was narrated by a group, and al-Hakim authenticated it, from Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn 'Adi, al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman*, and Ibn 'Asakir related from al-Dahhak that he said: their betrayal was slander (*namimah*). Its completion in one narration is: whenever Allah, exalted is He, revealed something, they would disclose it to the polytheists. Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jurayj that he said: their betrayal was that they were both disbelievers and opponents. It was also said: they were both hypocrites. Betrayal (*khiyanah*) and hypocrisy (*nifaq*) are one, according to al-Raghib, except that betrayal is used with regard to covenant and trust, and hypocrisy is used with regard to religion; then they overlap. So betrayal is opposing the truth by breaking a covenant in secret, and its opposite is trustworthiness (*amanah*). What is in the verse is interpreted in this sense, and it is not to be interpreted here as fornication (*fujur*), because of what more than one related from Ibn 'Abbas: "The wife of a prophet never committed adultery at all," and its ascription (*raf'uhu*) is from Ashras to the Prophet, may Allah exalt his mention and grant him peace. In *al-Kashshaf* it says: it is not permissible that fornication be intended by it, because it is vile in nature, a defect in the eyes of everyone, unlike disbelief, for people do not find disbelief vile, and they call it truth.

Ibn 'Atiyyah related from some of its interpreters that it is interpreted as disbelief, adultery, and other things. By my life, none would say this except the son of adultery. So the truth in my view is that the adultery of wives is like the adultery of mothers, among the repugnant things which, al-Sa'd said, it is correct to prevent in the case of the prophets, peace be upon them. What is attributed to the Shi'ah that contradicts this regarding the master of the prophets, may Allah exalt his mention and grant him peace, is a lie against them, so do not rely upon it, even if it is widespread.

In this, according to what has been said, there is a depiction of the condition of the two women, which resembles the condition of the disbelievers in their betrayal of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah exalt his mention and grant him peace, through disbelief and disobedience, despite their complete ability to have faith and obedience.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so they did not avail them﴾ and so on, is an explanation of what their betrayal led to, that is: ﴿those two righteous servants and great prophets did not avail them﴾ ﴿against Allah﴾, that is, against His punishment, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿in anything﴾, that is, any benefit, or any protection from the punishment.

It was said to them both at their death or on the Day of Resurrection, and the past tense is used to indicate the certainty of its occurrence: ﴿Enter the Fire with those who enter.﴾ That is, with the rest of those who enter, from among the disbelievers, who have no kinship between them and the prophets, peace be upon them.

Many have mentioned that the intended point is to indicate that the disbelievers are punished for their disbelief, and are not shown consideration because of the kinship between them and the Prophet, may Allah exalt his mention and grant him peace. In this there is an allusion to the mothers of the believers and a warning to them that it will not benefit them if they commit what is forbidden to them, namely being under the marriage of the Prophet, may Allah exalt his mention and grant him peace. There is nothing in this that indicates that among them there is a disbeliever or a hypocrite, as Yusuf al-Awali, one of the later Imamiyyah, claimed. Glory be to You, this is a tremendous slander.

Mubashshir ibn 'Ubayd read *tughniya* with a *ta'* above, and it is related from them both with *bi-taqdir 'an nafsihima* (with the implied "concerning themselves"). Abu Hayyan said: there must be this implied addition, unless *'an* is made a noun like *hi* in *da' 'anka* (leave aside from you), for if it were a particle, that would involve transferring the verb which takes the attached pronoun as subject to its genitive pronoun, and that pronoun functions as an accusative pronoun, and that is not permissible. And there is discussion in this.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 66, verse 11:**

﴿And Allah sets forth an example for those who believe: the wife of Pharaoh.﴾ That is, He made her situation an example for the situation of the believers, in that the marriage tie to disbelievers does not harm them, since she was in this world under the wing of the greatest enemy of Allah, Exalted and Majestic is He, while she is in the highest chambers of Paradise. Her name was Asiyah daughter of Muzahim. The words of the Exalted, ﴿when she said﴾, are an adverbial phrase (*zarf*) governed by an omitted verb, meaning: "And Allah set forth an example for those who believe, the situation of the wife of Pharaoh, when she said: ﴿My Lord, build for me near You﴾." It has been said: that is, near Your mercy, because He, glorified is He, is exempt from place.

It is permitted that ﴿near You﴾ (*'indaka*) be a circumstantial phrase (*hal*) from the pronoun of the speaker, and that it be a circumstantial phrase from the Exalted's words ﴿a house﴾ (*baytan*), since it precedes it; had it come after it, it would have been an attributive (*sifah*). The Exalted's words ﴿in Paradise﴾ (*fi al-jannah*) are either an apposition (*badal*) or an explanatory apposition (*'atf bayan*) for the words ﴿near You﴾, or they are connected to the word ﴿build﴾ (*ibni*). She placed ﴿near You﴾ first for a subtle purpose, which, as in *al-Fusus* (*al-Fusus*, a work of Ibn 'Arabi), is an allusion to the saying: "The neighbour before the house." It is also permitted that what is meant by ﴿near You﴾ is the highest ranks of those brought near, because what is with Allah the Exalted is better, and because what is meant is nearness to the Throne, with ﴿near You﴾ meaning "near Your Throne and the seat of Your might." This, as has been said, is one of the possibilities regarding its grammatical analysis (*i'rab*), and it does not necessarily follow that it is an adverbial complement of the verb.

﴿And save me from Pharaoh﴾, that is, from Pharaoh's own wicked self and his oppressive authority. ﴿And his deed﴾, that is, and especially from his deed, which is disbelief, the worship of other than Allah the Exalted, torturing without cause, and other ugliness. The phrasing is in the style of the Exalted's words ﴿His angels and His messengers, and Jibril﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:98). It is permitted that what is meant by ﴿save me﴾ is "from the deed of Pharaoh," in which case it is of the style of "Zayd pleased me, and his generosity." The first is more eloquent, because it indicates seeking distance from his wicked self, as if his very essence were a punishment and a ruin from which deliverance is sought. Then deliverance from his deed was sought a second time, to alert to the fact that it is the greatest calamity. Some restricted his deed to his torturing (of believers), and it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it is intercourse, but what preceded is more fitting. ﴿And save me from the wrongdoing people﴾: from the Copts who followed him in wrongdoing, as said by Muqatil. al-Kalbi said: from the people of Egypt. It seems he meant the Copts as well. The verse clearly shows that she was a believer who affirmed the resurrection. Some have mentioned that she was the aunt of Musa, peace be upon him, who believed when she saw the staff swallow the falsehood, and Pharaoh tortured her.

Abu Ya'la and al-Bayhaqi reported with a sound chain of transmission from Abu Hurayrah that Pharaoh drove four stakes for his wife into her hands and feet, and whenever they (the torturers) dispersed from her, the angels, peace be upon them, would shade her. She said: ﴿My Lord, build for me near You a house in Paradise﴾, and so it was unveiled to her, her house in Paradise, which, as has been said, was of pearl. In the narration of Abd ibn Humayd from him, he drove four stakes for her, laid her on her back, placed a millstone upon her chest, and turned her to face the sun. She raised her head to the sky and said: ﴿My Lord, build for me...﴾ up to ﴿the wrongdoing people﴾, and Allah opened for her a view of her house in Paradise, and she saw it. It was also said that he was commanded to have a great rock dropped upon her, so she called upon Allah the Exalted, and He raised her soul, and the rock fell upon a body with no soul in it. It is reported from al-Hasan that Allah saved her with the noblest deliverance and raised her to Paradise, where she eats, drinks, and enjoys herself. Its apparent meaning is that she was raised with her body, but this is not sound.

In the verse there is evidence that seeking refuge in Allah the Exalted, turning to Him, Mighty and Majestic is He, and asking Him for deliverance from Him, Exalted is He, in times of trial and calamity, is among the ways of the righteous and the practice of the prophets. This is abundant in the Qur'an.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 66, verse 12:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Mary, daughter of ʿImran﴾ is a conjunction with ﴿the wife of Pharaoh﴾, meaning: and He struck as a parable for those who believe the condition of her and what she was given of honour in this world and the Hereafter, and of being chosen, despite most of her people being disbelievers. He combined in the parable between one who has a husband and one who has no husband, as a consolation to widows and a comforting of their hearts, according to what has been said, and this is among the novel (bida') interpretations, as in the Kashshaf. Al-Sikhtiyani read ﴿ibnah﴾ with the ha' silent when connected, treating it as if in pause. ﴿Who guarded her chastity (farj)﴾: she preserved it and prevented it from men. And it was said: she kept it from the filth of sin.

The farj is what lies between the two legs, and it was used as a euphemism for the private part, and it became common until it was like an explicit term; and from it is what is here according to most of them. ﴿So We breathed into it﴾: the one who breathes is His messenger, exalted is He, and he is Gabriel, peace be upon him, so the attribution is metaphorical. It was also said: the speech is with an elision of a modifier, meaning: so Our messenger breathed, and the pronoun in ﴿fihi﴾ refers to the farj. It is well known that Gabriel, peace be upon him, breathed into her collar (jayb), and the effect of that reached the farj.

This is related from Qatadah. Al-Farra' said: the exegetes mentioned that the farj is the collar of her shirt (dir'), and this is possible, because the farj in linguistic meaning is every gap between two things, and the place of the collar of a woman's shirt is slit, so it is a farj. This is more eloquent in praise of her, for if she guarded the collar of her shirt, she is even more protective of herself. In Majma' al-Bayan, from al-Farra', it is said that the meaning is that she guarded the collar of her shirt from Gabriel, peace be upon him, and that this was, as has been said, her saying: ﴿Indeed, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are God-fearing﴾ [Maryam: 18]. The statement of some indicates that ﴿ahsanat farjaha﴾, according to what was first transmitted from al-Farra', is a metaphor for chastity, like the saying of people: he is clean of collar and pure of hem.

It is permitted that the pronoun in ﴿fihi﴾ refers to the foetus (ḥaml), which is Jesus, peace be upon him, implied by the speech. ʿAbdullah [ibn Masʿud] read ﴿fiha﴾, as in al-Anbiya', so the pronoun refers to Mary. The attribution in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from Our spirit﴾ is for honour, and what is meant is a spirit that We created without intermediary of origin. It was also said: for the slightest connection, but this is not the case.

﴿And she confirmed﴾: she believed ﴿in the words of her Lord﴾: in His scriptures, mighty and majestic, sent down upon Idris, peace be upon him, and others. He, glorified is He, called them words because of their brevity, ﴿and His books﴾: in all of His books. What is meant by it is other than the scrolls (suhuf), of which there is length; or the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms. The Mushaf is counted among those. Her belief in it, though it had not yet been sent down, is like belief in the awaited Prophet, prayers and peace be upon him, for he, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, was mentioned in his book in the three books. Interpreting the words and books in this way is what a group has chosen. Many others permitted that by the words is meant what God, exalted is He, revealed to His prophets, peace be upon them, and by the books what is known in them, which includes the scrolls and others. It was also said: all that is written, which includes the Preserved Tablet and others. And it is possible that by the words is meant His promise and His threat, or that and His command, mighty and majestic is He, and His prohibition, glorified is He; and by the books is meant one of the earlier aspects. But meaning by the words His eternal speech subsisting in His essence, glorified is He, is very far-fetched. Ya'qub, Abu Mijlaz, Qatadah and ʿIsmah from ʿAsim read ﴿saddaqat﴾ with lightness, and it returns to the meaning of the doubled form. In al-Bahr: that is, she was truthful in what she reported concerning the matter of Jesus and what God, exalted is He, made manifest to her of miracles. In this there is a deficiency that is not hidden.

Al-Hasan, Mujahid and al-Jahdari read ﴿bi-kalimatin﴾ in the singular. It is possible that it is a noun of genus, or that it refers to the word of tawhid, or that it refers to Jesus, peace be upon him, for he, peace be upon him, was called the Word of God which He cast to Mary, and this has been explained before. Many of the Seven read ﴿wa-kitabihi﴾ in the singular. It is possible that it means the genus, or that it means the Gospel, especially if the word is interpreted as Jesus, peace be upon him. Abu Raja' read ﴿wa-kutbihi﴾ with a silent ta', according to what Ibn ʿAtiyyah said, and with it and with a fatha on the kaf, on the basis that it is a verbal noun, the noun being put in its place, according to what the author of al-Lawami' said.

﴿And she was of the devout (al-qanitin)﴾: that is, among the number of those constant in obedience. The ﴿min﴾ is partitive, and the masculine form is for predominance, and to indicate that her obedience did not fall short of the obedience of men, so that she was counted among them. Thus it is more eloquent than our saying: "and she was of the female devout," or "devout (feminine)." It was also said: ﴿min﴾ is for the beginning of the limit, and what is meant is that she was of the descendants of the devout, for she was of the descendants of Aaron, brother of Moses, peace be upon them both. Her praise with this is because it is generally the case that the branch follows its root: ﴿And the good land, its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord, and that which is bad comes forth only sparingly﴾ [al-A'raf: 58]. She is, according to some reports, the lady of women and among the most perfect of them. Ahmad related in his Musnad: "The lady of the women of the people of Paradise is Mary, then Fatimah, then Khadijah, then Asiyah, then ʿA'ishah." In the Sahih: "Many men have attained perfection, but among women only four have attained it: Asiyah bint Muzahim, the wife of Pharaoh; Mary daughter of ʿImran; Khadijah bint Khuwaylid; and Fatimah bint Muhammad, may God's blessings and peace be upon him. And the excellence of ʿA'ishah over women is like the excellence of thareed over other food." Thareed, which is bread placed in broth with meat upon it, is singled out, as has been said:

When bread is seasoned with meat, that is the trust of God, the thareed.

Not meat alone, as has been said, because the Arabs prefer nothing over it, to the point that they called it the center of Paradise (buhbuhat al-jannah). The secret of it, according to al-Tibi, is that thareed with meat combines nourishment, pleasure, strength, ease of consumption, little effort in chewing, and swift passage through the gullet. So it was struck as a parable to indicate that she, may God be pleased with her, was given, along with good character, sweetness of speech, eloquence of tongue, excellence of wit, soundness of judgement, firmness of intellect, and endearment to her husband; so she is fit for the husband in conversation, companionship, enjoying her company, and listening to her. It is sufficient that she understood from the Prophet ﷺ what no other women understood, and related what none of the men like her related. As for the greater excellence she has in this noble surah, through the rebuke of her and of her companion Hafsah, may God be pleased with them both, it is not hidden. Then it is not hidden that Fatimah, may God be pleased with her, in terms of being the daughter of the Prophet, no one is counted equal to her in excellence, and the full discussion of that is in its proper place.

It has come in some reports that Mary and Asiyah are two wives of the Messenger of God ﷺ in Paradise. Al-Tabarani related from Sa'd ibn Junadah, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Indeed God married me in Paradise to Mary daughter of ʿImran, and the wife of Pharaoh, and the sister of Moses, peace be upon him." As for the claim of their prophethood, like the claim of the prophethood of other women such as Hajar and Sarah, it is not correct, since maleness is a condition of prophethood according to the sound view, unlike al-Ash'ari. This claim was pointed out by the scholar Ibn Qasim in al-Ayat al-Bayyinat, and it is strange, so let it be noted. And God knows best.
